content: The management system for morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) is based on community home care. The stakeholders involved in implementing and supervising MMDP may include the following: 1. Community-based care organizations: These include health workers, women’s groups, and youth groups. Their involvement should be supervised to ensure proper implementation of care activities. 2. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs): Their participation should be coordinated and supervised to align with the program’s goals. 3. Individuals with or without expertise in community-based care: These individuals are essential for ensuring proper organization and coordination of activities. 4. Religious and community leaders: Their involvement can help foster trust and engagement within the community. 5. Traditional healers and members of faith-based organizations: These individuals can play a role in culturally sensitive care delivery. Programs may also establish teams of individuals interested in improving the health and well-being of lymphatic filariasis (LF) patients in their communities. These teams could include representatives from local NGOs, community-based care organizations, or volunteers from women’s groups, support groups, self-help groups, youth groups, or cooperative groups. The team’s membership should broadly represent the community to ensure inclusivity. Advocacy and Social Mobilization Advocacy and social mobilization efforts should be implemented at various levels to promote MMDP activities. These efforts aim to ensure smooth program operation and the involvement of all relevant stakeholders. Examples of advocacy and communication activities include: Policy-level advocacy: Targeting health sector decision-makers, donors, policymakers, community leaders, religious leaders, opinion leaders, and teachers. Methods such as policy briefs, success stories, and targeted messages can increase knowledge, awareness, and support for prevention activities, budget allocation, and coordination. Program-level collaboration: Engaging program managers, doctors, nurses, and public health workers through success stories and messages to enhance collaboration in operations, monitoring, and evaluation. Research-level engagement: Involving medical laboratories and research scientists in forum discussions to advance research efforts. Community-level awareness: Training community health workers and volunteers to raise awareness and commitment through education and communication materials. Public education: Informing the general community, including schoolchildren, about health practices to prevent morbidity and disability. National programs may also conduct broader social mobilization campaigns depending on factors such as disease burden, hygiene practices, stigma levels, and available resources. Social mobilization can inform the population about the disease, modify attitudes (especially regarding stigma), and encourage early screening and active participation in case identification. It can also promote hygiene practices to prevent acute episodes and increase compliance with mass drug administration. Developing a social mobilization strategy requires specialized skills, and it is recommended that programs collaborate with experts in this field. Campaigns targeting local leaders should foster a sense of ownership and empowerment within the community to ensure the sustainability of MMDP activities with minimal input from the health system. Capacity Building and Training Strengthening the capacities of health staff at various levels and community members is critical for the success of MMDP. Examples of capacity-building activities include: Program managers and staff: Training in advocacy, inter-sectoral communication, program planning, clinical management techniques, and monitoring and evaluation. Resources include WHO manuals, regional training, and reporting systems. Health facility staff: Training in clinical management techniques, health promotion, and monitoring. Resources include WHO tools, case management guidelines, patient education materials, and medications. Community health workers and volunteers: Training in basic management techniques, health promotion, and social mobilization. Resources include WHO tools and patient education materials. Patients: Training in self-care techniques and access to medications and support groups. Standard operating procedures and training protocols for managing acute attacks, lymphedema (or elephantiasis), and hydrocele surgery should be established at the national level. Training materials may need to be adapted based on local knowledge, language, and literacy levels. Health care staff and caregivers should be trained to provide accurate information on self-care, contact points, and indications for hydrocelectomy. Training for Acute Attack and Lymphedema Management The steps for preparing a training program include: 1. Defining case management guidelines for identifying and managing acute attacks and lymphedema for physicians, health workers, and lay workers. 2. Preparing training curricula based on situational analysis of health staff competencies and needs. 3. Including modules on morbidity and disability due to LF in medical and nursing school curricula. Training materials should include a two-part module (tutor’s guide and learner’s guide), a flipchart for health care workers, and a poster for patients. WHO has developed a training package to assist regions and countries in planning, implementing, and evaluating MMDP activities. Psychological Support and Socioeconomic Rehabilitation Psychological support and socioeconomic rehabilitation are essential to complement medical and surgical care. These efforts help patients overcome stigma and shame, enabling full integration into their communities. Actions to prevent stigma include: Discussing the relevance of psychological support with health counselors. Establishing referral systems for psychological support services. Identifying and providing necessary training materials for health care staff, community health workers, and patients. Socioeconomic rehabilitation may involve assisting patients in finding suitable jobs, as disabilities associated with lymphedema and hydrocele often lead to an inability to work. However, these activities may fall outside the scope of LF program staff and depend on available human and financial resources. Even if such support is unavailable, other MMDP activities should not be delayed. For further guidance, resources such as the WHO’s Community-Based Rehabilitation Guidelines and the International Federation of Anti-Leprosy Associations’ Stigma and Mental Wellbeing Guides can be consulted.
